title: How do you use the rule of 72 to estimate how long something takes to double?
description: The rule of 72: a quick way to do this case calculation in your head, with a worked example.
hook: Divide 72 by the yearly growth rate in percent, and the answer is roughly how many years something takes to double. At 8% a year, 72 ÷ 8 gives 9 years, and the exact answer is 9.01. It is quick, accurate enough for any case at normal growth rates, and works backwards too.
body:
The rule

A market grows 8% a year. How long until it doubles?
  1. Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth rate (in %).
  2. 72 ÷ 8 = 9.
  3. Answer: about 9 years.

It works the other way too. Growth rate needed ≈ 72 ÷ years. To double in six years, a business needs about 72 ÷ 6 = 12% a year.

How to say it in the interview

"Using the rule of 72, at 8% a year the market doubles in about nine years. So the $500M market today is roughly $1B by the early 2030s, which makes the client's ten-year target of $200M in sales about a 20% share of the future market."

Name the rule so the interviewer knows it is an approximation, then use the result for something. A doubling time on its own is a fact; a doubling time compared with the client's goal is an insight.

How accurate is it?

Very accurate between about 5% and 12%, and still close enough outside that range for a case.

Growth rateRule of 72Exact years to double
2%3635.0
5%14.414.2
8%9.09.0
10%7.27.3
15%4.85.0
20%3.63.8
30%2.42.6

At high rates the rule slightly understates the doubling time. If a big investment hinges on whether something doubles in 3.6 or 3.8 years, do the exact sum: years = ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + rate).

Why 72? It is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, so the division is almost always easy, and it happens to fit typical growth rates well.

Three useful extensions

Quadrupling

Two doublings. At 8% a year, something doubles in 9 years and quadruples in about 18.

Inflation

At 3% inflation, prices double, and the buying power of a fixed sum halves, in about 72 ÷ 3 = 24 years (23.4 exactly).

Decline

Be careful with shrinking businesses. Something falling 8% a year keeps 0.92 of its value each year, so it halves in ln(0.5) ÷ ln(0.92) = 8.3 years, not 9. The rule overstates the time to halve, so a declining business gets to half its size faster than the rule suggests.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing by the decimal. 72 ÷ 0.08 = 900. Use the percentage: 72 ÷ 8.
  • Mixing time units. A monthly rate gives a doubling time in months. 2% a month doubles in about 36 months.
  • Using it for one-off jumps. The rule assumes steady compound growth year after year.

Practice

1. Savings earn 6% a year. How long until they double?

Show the answer

72 ÷ 6 = about 12 years.

2. A client wants to double revenue in four years. What growth rate does it need?

Show the answer

72 ÷ 4 = about 18% a year. The exact answer is 18.9%, slightly higher, as the table predicts at higher rates. Then ask whether the market is growing that fast; if not, the client has to win share.

3. A $300M market grows 9% a year. Roughly how big is it in 16 years?

Show the answer

72 ÷ 9 = 8 years to double, so 16 years is two doublings: $300M → $600M → about $1.2B. The exact figure is $1.19B.

Where to practise next

For growth rates over a fixed period, read working out a yearly growth rate and compound growth and CAGR. The rule also helps with payback and NPV, and you can practise it under time pressure in the case maths drill.
